subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
passage: At lunch, a group of boys began imitating the new boy's accent. Everyone laughed, and Dolma laughed too, a bit too loudly. I was sitting across from her and noticed her laugh stopped at her mouth. Her eyes were on her tray. When the joke was repeated, she looked down and picked at her rice. I'm Sahil, and I can't say what was in her mind. Maybe she found it funny. Maybe she didn't. But when the group moved on, she said quietly, "I shouldn't have laughed." I said, "You didn't have to." She nodded.

qa.q: What did the group of boys imitate at lunch?
qa.a: They imitated the new boy's accent.

qa.q: What might Dolma have felt when she laughed too loudly, and what else could it be?
qa.a: She may have been uneasy and laughing to fit in, since her laugh stopped at her mouth and she said she shouldn't have laughed. Sahil admits she might also have found it funny.

qa.q: What could Dolma do next time a joke feels unkind?
qa.a: She can stay quiet or say calmly, "that's not funny," and sit with safer friends. Sahil's reply shows she doesn't have to laugh.

qa.q: How might the new boy have felt when everyone laughed?
qa.a: He probably felt singled out and hurt. He may not have known which laughs were real.

grounding: A teenager laughs along with a group joke that feels unkind, masking unease, and an observer notices.

subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
passage:
Monday: In the canteen, Vasudha laughed along when the others mocked Pooja's haircut. Pooja laughed too, though her eyes stayed flat. 
Wednesday: Pooja sat alone. Vasudha noticed and remembered the flat eyes. She felt her stomach turn.
Friday: Vasudha walked over. "I laughed on Monday and I shouldn't have. It wasn't funny." Pooja looked up. "I hated it. I laughed to fit in." "Me too," said Vasudha. "Next time I'll say 'that's not funny'." Pooja smiled, a real one this time. "Then I'll sit with you at lunch."

qa.q: On which day did Vasudha laugh along in the canteen?
qa.a: She laughed along on Monday.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when she laughed with flat eyes on Monday?
qa.a: She felt hurt and laughed to fit in. Her flat eyes and later sitting alone show it wasn't real amusement.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do differently the next time someone is mocked?
qa.a: She can say "that's not funny" calmly and sit with someone kind. That protects the boundary and the friendship.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see her own laugh by Friday?
qa.a: She regrets it and feels uneasy. Seeing Pooja's flat eyes made her realise it hurt.

grounding: A teenager hides hurt behind a laugh to fit in, and later a friend names a calm boundary.

subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
passage:
"Trisha, you asked why I don't laugh when your cousins make fun of people. Let your Harsha Mausi tell you.
When I was fifteen, my friends in Jaipur used to mimic a new girl's accent. She came from a village and said some words differently. Everyone laughed, and I laughed too. Loudly. But inside I felt sick. I wanted them to like me.
One day the girl heard. She looked at me, only at me, like she expected better. That night I couldn't sleep.
The next time they started, I said, very calmly, 'That's not funny.' They stared. A few stopped talking to me. But two others quietly agreed.
Those two are still my friends. The loud ones, I don't even remember their names."

qa.q: What did Harsha's friends mimic?
qa.a: A new girl's accent.

qa.q: What was young Harsha feeling while laughing along?
qa.a: She felt sick and uneasy inside, laughing only because she wanted to fit in.

qa.q: What choice inside the story was healthier for Harsha?
qa.a: Saying calmly "That's not funny" set a boundary and led her to safer, kinder friends.

qa.q: How might the new girl have felt when Harsha laughed?
qa.a: The new girl probably felt hurt and let down, especially by Harsha, from whom she expected better.

grounding: An aunt recalls laughing along with an unkind joke to fit in and choosing a calm boundary and safer friends.

subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
passage:
The school bus was packed on the rainy afternoon, and Salma was squashed in a seat near the back with the loud group. One of the boys started joking about Afreen's father, who sweeps the school corridors. "Hey Afreen, does your dad sweep your house too?"
The group burst out laughing. Salma laughed too, a little, without thinking.
Then she saw Afreen, two seats ahead, staring out the steamed-up window, her jaw tight.
Salma's laugh died. She felt sick. She couldn't move away, the bus was too crowded.
She took a breath. "That's not funny," she said, calmly.
The boy stared. "Chill, it's a joke."
"Not to her," Salma said.
The group went quiet. At Afreen's stop, Salma squeezed past and sat next to her for the last few minutes.

qa.q: What job does Afreen's father do?
qa.a: He sweeps the school corridors.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when her laugh died?
qa.a: Salma felt sick and ashamed, realising she had laughed at something that hurt her friend.

qa.q: What did Salma do that was healthier than laughing along?
qa.a: She calmly said "That's not funny" and then sat with Afreen, choosing kindness over fitting in.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt when Salma spoke up?
qa.a: Afreen probably felt supported and less alone, even after the hurtful joke.

grounding: On a crowded bus, a teenager laughs along with an unkind joke, then chooses a calm boundary instead.

subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
passage:
At a birthday party in a Pune flat, some boys started joking about Mohit's height. "Hey shorty, can you see the cake?" Everyone laughed. Mohit laughed the loudest, pretending it was funny.
But his friend Wasim noticed. Mohit's laugh was too loud, and his hands were shoved deep in his pockets.
Later, on the stairs, Wasim asked, "You okay?"
Mohit shrugged. "I always laugh. Otherwise they'll think I can't take a joke."
"But does it feel funny?"
Mohit was quiet. "No. It feels bad every time."
Wasim nodded. "Next time, maybe just say it's not funny. I'll back you."
Mohit looked at him. "You really would?"
"Obviously."

qa.q: What did the boys call Mohit?
qa.a: "Shorty."

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling behind his loud laugh?
qa.a: Mohit felt hurt and uneasy, laughing to hide it and to fit in.

qa.q: What did Wasim suggest?
qa.a: Wasim suggested Mohit say "that's not funny" next time, and promised to back him up.

qa.q: How did Wasim see Mohit's laugh?
qa.a: Wasim noticed it was too loud and paired with hands in pockets, a sign of masking hurt rather than real amusement.

grounding: At a party, a teenager laughs to mask hurt, and a friend helps him choose a calm boundary.

subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
passage:
"Tarun, is that phone from a museum?" Vikram held it up. "Does it take calls from the dinosaurs?"
The group roared. Kishore laughed too, a beat late and a little too loud.
Tarun laughed loudest of all. "Ha, yeah, my Jurassic phone."
"Does it run on coal?" someone added.
"Probably!" Tarun's laugh went higher. He took the phone back and put it face down.
Kishore's stomach tightened. Last week Tarun had told him his dad had lost his job.
"Okay," Kishore said, not loudly. "That's not funny anymore. Come on, the match starts in five."
Vikram rolled his eyes. "Relax, it's a joke."
"It was a joke three jokes ago."
On the way to the ground, Tarun fell into step beside him. "Thanks," he muttered. "I didn't know how to stop laughing."

qa.q: What did Vikram ask whether the phone could take calls from?
qa.a: The dinosaurs.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling as he laughed a beat late?
qa.a: Kishore felt uneasy and tense, laughing to fit in while knowing the joke touched something painful for Tarun.

qa.q: What made Kishore's boundary work?
qa.a: He said calmly, not loudly, that it wasn't funny anymore and gave everyone somewhere to go, without shaming anyone.

qa.q: What was the joking like for Tarun?
qa.a: It hurt, but Tarun laughed loudest to protect his place in the group and didn't know how to stop.

grounding: It illustrates teenagers laughing along with an unkind group joke to fit in or hide hurt, and one of them setting a calm 'that's not funny' boundary.
